title: The peace churches
hook: Mennonites, Quakers and Brethren refuse to fight, following Matthew 5:39

segments.voice: Yesterday, just war: Augustine and Aquinas drawing lines around fighting, a just cause, a last resort, civilians kept out of it. Your line was war has limits. Where did you see a limit hold? Day one thousand two hundred twelve.

A young man stands in front of a draft board with a Bible under his arm. He isn't dodging hard work. He'll drive an ambulance, fight forest fires, empty bedpans on a hospital ward. The one thing he won't do is carry a rifle. When they ask him why, he opens to the Sermon on the Mount and reads a single sentence out loud. Yesterday we heard Christians who say a war can be just, inside strict limits. Today, the Christians who answer: not for us. Mennonites, Quakers, the Brethren. The peace churches.

The sentence he reads is Matthew 5:39, in the King James Bible: "But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also." The peace churches take that as plain instruction for ordinary life, and they don't carve out an exception for war. They point to the night Jesus was arrested. One of his followers draws a sword, and Jesus answers with the line we heard yesterday, which the peace churches read as a rule for their own lives: "Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword." Then he walks toward the cross without a fight. Now notice what turning the cheek is not. It isn't running away, and it isn't shrugging. The person who turns the other cheek is still standing there, face to face. Paul puts the same move into one line in Romans: "Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good." So the peace churches pair the refusal with action: relief work after floods and wars, rebuilding houses, sitting between two sides of a quarrel. Quakers call their stance a testimony, something a life says out loud. Christians in the just war tradition read the same sermon and conclude that protecting the weak can sometimes require force. This path won't rank them. Each side hands the other a hard question: who protects the neighbor, and what does it cost to turn the cheek? And both hear the same sermon go on: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you."

Here's the practice: nonviolence, sized small. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one little conflict you're in right now: a sharp text thread, a roommate, a coworker, a sibling. Notice the move you'd usually make to win it. The cutting reply. The silent treatment. Now try the peace churches' question. What would it look like to stay standing there, not striking back and not walking off, and do one good thing instead? A softer answer. A real question. Just picture it. If you pray, you can hold that person before God. The bell holds the time.
The peace churches. Mennonites, Quakers and Brethren, who read turn the other cheek as a word for all of life, and refuse to fight while working for peace.
Your line: the peaceable way. Today, in one small conflict, don't strike back, in words or otherwise. Answer with one good thing instead. Day one thousand two hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Mennonite, Quaker and Brethren congregations teach nonviolence as part of following Jesus; members have sought to serve as conscientious objectors rather than bear arms, and these churches run relief, rebuilding and peacemaking work.

fork.setup: you're the young man at the draft board. your church reads Matthew 5:39 as a plain command. what do you do?
options: carry the rifle and keep your faith private.
refuse the rifle and offer to serve another way.
fork.reveal: the peace churches teach both halves: refuse to fight, and serve anyway. turning the cheek means staying in the room, not leaving it.

original.note: Greek, Matthew 5:39: to stand against, to resist. "resist not evil."

trapdoor: what you thought: turn the other cheek means be a doormat.
what it means: refuse to strike back, stay face to face, and overcome evil with good. the peace churches pair the refusal with service.
what a scholar hears: antistenai, to stand against. some readers argue Jesus forbids striking back in kind, not standing up at all.

notes: The draft-board scene is a composite illustration of conscientious objection, not a named historical person; confirm it reads as such and that the alternative-service examples (ambulance, firefighting, hospital work) are fair.

The peace churches' practice (relief work, rebuilding, mediation) is described without naming organizations, dates or numbers; confirm the description is fair to Mennonite, Quaker and Brethren self-understanding.
'Quakers call their stance a testimony' refers to the Quaker peace testimony; confirm the gloss 'something a life says out loud'.
Just war tradition summarized as concluding that protecting the weak can sometimes require force; confirm fair, and that the two positions are presented without ranking.
Trapdoor: the reading of antistenai as 'do not retaliate in kind' (associated with some modern interpreters) is attributed only to 'some readers'; confirm the hedging is adequate.
